title: Severe headache, fever and neck stiffness in an 18-year-old student
desc: This station involves a time-critical focused history and examination of an 18-year-old unvaccinated student brought to the ED by ambulance with a 4-hour severe headache, fever, photophobia and neck stiffness. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, bloods and CSF results, diagnoses pneumococcal bacterial meningitis, manages it in the ED according to eTG, and answers her questions about migraine and whether her family can catch it.
focus: Acute headache with fever: separating meningitis from other causes of headache, starting treatment without delay, and interpreting the CSF
stem: You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital in Melbourne. Jamie Hunt, an 18-year-old Year 12 student, has been brought in by ambulance with a severe headache. She is lying on a trolley in an acute bay with monitoring attached. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jamie and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think she needs as you go (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Jamie's observations, blood results and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jamie Hunt, 18, a Year 12 student. You feel really unwell. You lie still with your eyes half shut because the light hurts, and you wince if your head is moved. You are fully alert and answer clearly, but you sound flat and miserable. If the candidate dims the lights or gives you something for the pain or nausea, you settle a little and say so ("That's a bit better, thanks"). The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I feel really unwell doctor, and I've got this awful headache."

The headache (give only when asked)

  • It started about 4 hours ago (about 10 am). It came on over a while, not suddenly. It has been constant and has got steadily worse.
  • It is all over your head and does not go anywhere else. It is an aching pain, 8/10.
  • You took paracetamol at home, which did not help. Light makes it worse.
  • It is not worse when you lie down or stand up, not worse when you cough or strain, and you did not wake with it.
  • It is not the worst headache of your life coming on in seconds, like being hit on the head. You have had no warning headache in the days or weeks before.
  • You have never had headaches like this before. No flashing lights, zigzags or other warning before it started.

Other symptoms (give when asked)

  • You have felt feverish: hot and cold, with some shakes.
  • Your neck is stiff and sore to bend.
  • You feel sick and have vomited once.
  • You have not eaten or drunk much today because you feel so sick. You have passed less urine than usual.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No rash or spots anywhere.
  • No fits, no confusion, no memory problems. No cold or flu-like illness beforehand. No earache, sinus pain, sore throat or cough.
  • No head injury or fall.
  • No dizziness or spinning, no weakness or numbness of the face, arms or legs, no pins and needles, no change in walking, no slurred speech.
  • No blurred or double vision, no red or painful eye, no seeing halos around lights, no whooshing in the ears.
  • No pain in the jaw when chewing, no tenderness of the scalp or temples. No clicking or pain in the jaw joint. No watering of one eye or runny nose on one side.
  • No band-like tightness around the head. No weight loss.

Risks for infection (only if asked)

  • Vaccines: "I can't remember ever having any vaccines in my life."
  • You have never had your spleen removed. You do not take steroids or anything that lowers your immunity.
  • No recent overseas or interstate travel.

Past medical history

  • Nothing. No operations. No immunisations. No travel.

Medications and allergies

  • The oral contraceptive pill, taken every day. No other medicines, no supplements, no recreational drugs.
  • No allergies.
  • If asked: your last period was 2 weeks ago and you do not think you could be pregnant.

Family history

  • Nothing significant. Your cousin gets migraines.

Social history

  • Never smoked. About 2 standard drinks a day on weekends.
  • Year 12 student doing your VCE. You live with your parents and are well supported. You do not feel stressed.
  • CrossFit twice a week and a healthy diet.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "Do I have a migraine? I have a cousin who has migraines."
  • Concerns: you cannot focus on your VCE study.
  • Expectations: "Please just make me feel better." "I just want to know what's going on."

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • The nurse gives the observations and a bedside glucose when asked (see Exam findings).
  • If the candidate orders anything (cannula, bloods, blood cultures, fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, dexamethasone, antibiotics, CT, lumbar puncture), the nurse says "I'll get that started." If no dose is given, the nurse asks "What dose would you like?"
  • If the candidate asks for a CT brain, the nurse asks once: "Does she need the CT before the lumbar puncture?" Let the candidate answer.
  • If the candidate has not asked for any treatment or investigations by halfway, the nurse says: "She looks really unwell. Is there anything you'd like me to do?"
  • If the candidate asks for blood or CSF results, the nurse says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: flushed, unwell, lying still with eyes half closed, photophobic. Dry mucous membranes. Weight 60 kg.
  • Observations: RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 112/68, HR 116 regular, temperature 39.2 °C, CRT 2 seconds, pain 8/10. BGL 5.4 mmol/L.
  • Conscious state: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6), oriented, no confusion.
  • Skin: no rash, no petechiae and no purpura anywhere, including the legs, trunk, palms, soles and conjunctivae.
  • Meningism: neck stiffness (resists passive neck flexion). Kernig's sign positive. Brudzinski's sign positive. Photophobia.
  • Fundoscopy: sharp optic discs, no papilloedema.
  • Cranial nerves: pupils 4 mm, equal and reactive. Visual fields full. Eye movements full, no nystagmus or diplopia. Face symmetrical. Normal hearing to whisper.
  • Limbs: tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. No pronator drift. Plantars flexor. Coordination normal. Gait not tested (too unwell to stand).
  • Head, eyes, ears and face: no signs of head injury. Eyes white, corneas clear. Temporal arteries non-tender and pulsatile. Jaw joints non-tender. Sinuses non-tender. Tympanic membranes normal. Throat normal.
  • Cardiovascular: HR 116 regular, heart sounds dual, no murmur. Peripheries warm.
  • Respiratory: chest clear.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. No scars.
  • Urine pregnancy test (if asked): negative.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Jamie's identity and gains consent before examining.
Recognises an unwell patient: acknowledges her pain, dims the lights or offers analgesia and an antiemetic early, uses plain language and keeps the history focused.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Onset 4 hours ago, building up over time (not thunderclap), constant and progressively worse
Paracetamol has not helped; worse with light; not positional, not worse with cough or in the morning

check.x: Elicits the associated features of meningitis: subjective fevers with shakes, neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea with one vomit, and poor oral intake.
Specifically asks about a rash (none).
Screens for subarachnoid and other intracranial haemorrhage: sudden (thunderclap) onset or worst-ever headache, a sentinel headache, and head trauma.

Screens for encephalitis, stroke and raised intracranial pressure: seizures, confusion or memory change, preceding flu-like illness, vertigo, facial or limb weakness, paraesthesia, gait change, visual disturbance, and headache on waking or with coughing.

Asks targeted questions for at least four other causes: migraine (aura, previous headaches), cluster, tension-type, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, giant cell arteritis or angle-closure glaucoma (and says they are unlikely at her age), TMJ dysfunction, tumour, dehydration or hypoglycaemia.
Asks about risk factors for meningitis:

kids.x: Immunisation status: cannot recall any vaccines in her life

check.x: Takes the past history, medications and allergies:

kids.x: Oral contraceptive pill; no other medicines, supplements or recreational drugs
No drug allergies, checked before antibiotics are given
Last period and the possibility of pregnancy

check.x: Takes the family history (nil; cousin with migraine) and social history: non-smoker, 2 standard drinks a day on weekends, VCE student living with supportive parents, CrossFit, healthy diet.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it may be migraine like her cousin, worried about VCE study, wants to feel better and know what is going on.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a BGL, and notes fever 39.2 °C, HR 116 and a normal BGL of 5.4 mmol/L.
Assesses conscious state by GCS components (E4 V5 M6 = 15) and checks pupils.
Inspects the whole skin for a petechial or purpuric (non-blanching) rash.
Examines for meningism and identifies neck stiffness, a positive Kernig's sign and a positive Brudzinski's sign.
Looks for focal signs and raised intracranial pressure: fundoscopy (no papilloedema), cranial nerves and a limb neurological screen, all normal.
Assesses hydration and looks for a source and mimics in at least three areas: mucous membranes and CRT, ears, sinuses and throat, chest, eyes (red eye for glaucoma) and temporal arteries.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: fever in the yellow zone on arrival; by 15:05 RR 26, systolic BP 96, HR 128 and temperature 39.6 °C are all yellow zone with a rising trend, meaning worsening sepsis that needs clinical review and senior escalation now, with ICU review.

Interprets the bloods: neutrophilia, CRP 186 and lactate 2.8 with a metabolic acidosis show sepsis with hypoperfusion; raised urea fits dehydration; normal glucose; normal platelets and coagulation meant the LP was safe; negative hCG.
Interprets the CSF:

kids.x: Turbid fluid, raised opening pressure, neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis (WCC 2400, 90% polymorphs), raised protein and a low glucose (calculates a CSF:plasma ratio of about 0.2): a bacterial pattern
Gram-positive diplococci indicate Streptococcus pneumoniae, with culture and susceptibilities pending
Minimal red cells argue against subarachnoid haemorrhage

check.x: Gives the diagnosis as bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with sepsis, with supporting features.
Names the differentials with a feature against each: meningococcal disease, viral meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage and migraine.
Management
In Part 1, once fever and meningism are found, asks the nurse for blood cultures and immediate dexamethasone and IV ceftriaxone, without waiting for CT or LP.
check.d: Credit only if ordered during Part 1.

check.x: Orders the work-up: BGL, FBC, UEC, CRP, VBG with lactate, coagulation, blood cultures before antibiotics, and LP. States that CT before LP is needed only for a contraindication (reduced GCS, focal signs, seizures, papilloedema), none of which Jamie has.
check.d: Credit if ordered in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Resuscitates: DRSABCD, IV access, IV crystalloid bolus with reassessment for the falling BP, oxygen only if SpO2 falls, and senior ED and ICU review.
Gives the eTG regimen:

kids.x: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, then 6-hourly for 4 days, continued because the organism is pneumococcus
Discusses with ID: vancomycin added while Gram-positive diplococci are awaiting susceptibilities, then directed therapy

check.x: Gives symptom relief: IV paracetamol and titrated IV opioid, an antiemetic such as ondansetron, and a dim, quiet bay.
Notifies public health (invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable) and states that close contacts do not need prophylaxis for pneumococcus, unlike meningococcal disease.
Admits under medicine or ID (ICU if she keeps deteriorating) with hourly neurological observations and fluid balance.
Explains to Jamie in plain words that this is not a migraine but a bacterial infection of the lining of the brain, that her family does not need antibiotics, and answers her VCE concern with empathy.
Safety netting
Sets escalation triggers for the nurses: a fall in GCS or new confusion, seizure, new focal weakness or unequal pupils, a new rash, falling BP or rising HR, and worsening headache or vomiting.
Tells Jamie in plain words to tell a nurse straight away about a worse headache, feeling drowsy or confused, a fit, weakness, a new rash, or a change in vision or hearing.
Arranges follow-up: a hearing test, catch-up vaccination with her GP, GP review after discharge, and support for her VCE (special consideration).

part2.lead: It is now 15:15. The ED registrar performed a lumbar puncture at 14:40, after your assessment. Here are Jamie's observations since arrival, her blood results with a venous gas, and her CSF results.
part2.patient:
For the fourth question, as the candidate explains, ask these once each:

  • "So it's not a migraine?"
  • "Can Mum and Dad catch it? Do they need tablets?"
  • "Will I be able to do my exams?"

If the candidate uses jargon (meningitis, pneumococcus, CSF), ask: "Sorry, what does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Room air throughout. GCS 15 with pupils equal and reactive at each check. No rash seen at any check.
handover.model:
• Read: at 14:10 and 14:40 the temperature (39.2 to 39.4 °C) is in the yellow zone. HR 114 to 116, BP, RR and SpO2 are white, and the BGL is normal. At 15:05 RR 26, systolic BP 96, HR 128 and temperature 39.6 °C are all in the yellow zone, with the nurse concerned. GCS stays 15.
  • Meaning: her sepsis is getting worse: falling BP, rising heart and respiratory rates, and lactate 2.8 on the gas. No red zone value yet, but several yellow values that are all trending the wrong way.
  • Changes: yellow zone values call for a clinical review. With this trend she needs senior ED review now, a fluid bolus and reassessment, ICU review, and a rapid response if any value reaches the red zone or her GCS falls. Antibiotics and dexamethasone must already be in, or go in now.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: headache, fever, neck stiffness
Before LP: GCS 15, pupils equal, no rash
Repeat set: more lethargic, vomited again; GCS 15, no rash

handover.label: Bloods and venous gas
handover.result: Collected 14:15 at cannulation. Blood cultures (2 sets, 14:15): no growth to date. Coagulation results were available before the LP.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 22.4 with neutrophilia 19.8 and CRP 186. Venous pH 7.31, bicarbonate 19, base excess -5 and lactate 2.8: a mild lactic metabolic acidosis. Urea 8.1 with a normal creatinine. Glucose 5.6. Platelets, INR and APTT normal. β-hCG not pregnant.
  • Meaning: a severe bacterial infection with sepsis and early hypoperfusion. The raised urea with a normal creatinine fits dehydration from poor intake and vomiting. No hypoglycaemia.
  • Changes: normal platelets and coagulation confirm the LP was safe. Fluid resuscitation and a repeat lactate. Ceftriaxone needs no renal adjustment. Blood cultures continue and may grow the organism.

handover.label: CSF results
handover.result: Jamie Hunt, UR 1256778. Lumbar puncture 14:40, left lateral position, opening pressure measured. Cell count and Gram stain reported 15:10. Culture and antibiotic susceptibilities pending (final at 48 hours). Pneumococcal and meningococcal PCR pending.
handover.model:
• Read: opening pressure raised at 34 cmH2O. Turbid, cloudy fluid. WCC 2400 ×106/L, 90% neutrophils. Red cells 3 (minimal). Protein raised at 2.1 g/L. CSF glucose 1.2 with a paired plasma glucose of 5.8: the candidate calculates a ratio of about 0.21 (low). Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. Culture pending.
  • Meaning: turbid CSF with a high neutrophil count, high protein and low glucose is the bacterial pattern. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae. Meningococci are Gram-negative diplococci. Minimal red cells argue against subarachnoid haemorrhage. A viral pattern would be clear fluid, lymphocytes and a normal glucose.
  • Changes: pneumococcal meningitis: continue dexamethasone for 4 days with ceftriaxone, and add vancomycin while susceptibilities are pending, with ID input. Narrow to directed therapy once susceptibilities return. Notify public health. Close contacts need no prophylaxis.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jamie Hunt, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jamie now, here in the emergency department.
Jamie asks you, "So is it a migraine, and can my family catch it?" Please answer her, then tell her what to watch for and what follow-up she will need.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Jamie Hunt, 18, UR 1256778.
  • Situation: bacterial meningitis with Gram-positive diplococci in the CSF (likely pneumococcal), and worsening sepsis: yellow zone at 15:05.
  • Background: 4 hours of a progressive generalised headache, fevers with shakes, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; unvaccinated; OCP only, no drug allergies.
  • Assessment: T 39.6, HR 128, BP 96/56, RR 26, GCS 15, no rash, Kernig's and Brudzinski's positive, no focal signs or papilloedema. WCC 22.4, CRP 186, lactate 2.8 with acidosis, urea 8.1 (dehydrated), coagulation normal. CSF turbid, OP 34, WCC 2400 mostly neutrophils, protein 2.1, glucose ratio 0.21.
  • Recommendation: please review now; dexamethasone and ceftriaxone given or going in now; ID advice on vancomycin; fluids; ICU review; admit.

Bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, with sepsis: fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's, unvaccinated; bacterial CSF pattern with Gram-positive diplococci.

  • Meningococcal disease: for: same picture, unvaccinated; against: no rash, and meningococci are Gram-negative diplococci.
  • Viral meningitis: for: young, fever, meningism; against: turbid neutrophilic CSF with a low glucose and organisms.
  • Encephalitis (HSV): against: GCS 15, no confusion, behaviour change or seizures.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: for: headache, neck stiffness; against: gradual onset, fever, minimal CSF red cells.
  • Migraine: for: photophobia, nausea, cousin has migraines; against: fever, meningism, first headache like this, no aura.

1. DRSABCD: senior ED review now for the yellow zone trend; second cannula; IV crystalloid bolus and reassess; oxygen only if SpO2 falls; ICU review.
  2. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose (give now if not already in), then 6-hourly for 4 days (continued because it is pneumococcal).
  3. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly, never delayed for imaging or LP; blood cultures already taken.
  4. Gram-positive diplococci: add vancomycin until susceptibilities return (eTG), with ID; then directed therapy.
  5. IV paracetamol, titrated IV opioid, ondansetron; dim bay.
  6. Hourly neurological observations, fluid balance, repeat lactate and sodium.
  7. Notify public health (invasive pneumococcal disease); no contact prophylaxis.
  8. Admit under medicine or ID (ICU if she deteriorates); catch-up vaccination and a hearing test later.

• Plain words: not a migraine; a bacterial infection of the lining around the brain and spinal cord (meningitis), caused by the pneumococcus germ; it needs antibiotics through a drip in hospital and steroid medicine to protect the brain and hearing.
  • Family: this germ does not spread like meningococcus; Mum and Dad do not need antibiotics; public health is told routinely.
  • Exams: recovery comes first; a letter for special consideration.
  • Tell a nurse straight away: worse headache, feeling drowsy or confused, a fit, weakness, a new rash, a change in vision or hearing.
  • Follow-up: a hearing test; catch-up vaccines with her GP; GP review after discharge; come back to ED for returning fever or worsening headache.

ddx.dx: Bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae
ddx.for: Four hours of a progressive headache with fever, rigors, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs in an unvaccinated 18-year-old, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, low glucose and Gram-positive diplococci.
She is a young unvaccinated adult with fever, meningism and worsening sepsis.
ddx.against: She has no petechial or purpuric rash, and the Gram stain shows Gram-positive, not Gram-negative, diplococci.

ddx.for: She has a severe headache with neck stiffness and photophobia.
ddx.against: The onset was gradual over hours, not thunderclap, she has a high fever, and the CSF has minimal red cells.
GCS 15 with no confusion, memory change, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs, and a bacterial CSF pattern.

ddx.for: She is young with fever, headache, photophobia and meningism.
ddx.against: The CSF is turbid with a neutrophil pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein and organisms on Gram stain.

ddx.for: She has photophobia, nausea and vomiting, and her cousin has migraines.
ddx.against: She has never had headaches like this, has no aura, is febrile with meningism, and paracetamol did not help.

guide:
This is an acute station. The examiner plays the nurse in Part 1. Give the observations and BGL when asked, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Give each system's findings as a block. If the candidate asks for blood or CSF results, say they will be given in Part 2. If the candidate asks for a CT, the nurse asks once whether it is needed before the LP; credit the answer under item 30. Item 29 is credited only if blood cultures and immediate dexamethasone and ceftriaxone are ordered during Part 1. If they are, accept "continue" in the answer to question 3 for item 32, but the doses must be given. Item 30 can be credited in either part. If the candidate has not ordered anything by halfway, give the nurse's prompt.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. For the fourth question the student playing Jamie asks the questions in the Part 2 script.

A high-performing candidate sees within the first minutes that this is fever with meningism. They ask about a rash, screen the dangerous and primary headache causes in clusters, find that she is unvaccinated, and check allergies. They examine the skin, meningism, GCS, pupils and fundi, and ask for blood cultures and immediate dexamethasone with ceftriaxone without waiting for CT or LP. In Part 2 they recognise the worsening yellow zone trend, read the CSF as bacterial with Gram-positive diplococci (pneumococcus), give the eTG doses, ask ID about vancomycin, notify public health, and know that contacts do not need prophylaxis.

A borderline candidate takes a long headache history without structure, forgets to ask about a rash or vaccination, or does not examine for meningism. They may order a CT before treating "to be safe", delay antibiotics until after the LP, leave out dexamethasone, call the CSF "abnormal" without a pattern, or offer prophylaxis to the family as if it were meningococcal disease.
explain:
Diagnosis: pneumococcal bacterial meningitis

Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia make up the classic picture of meningitis. Kernig's sign (pain or resistance when the knee is extended with the hip flexed) and Brudzinski's sign (the hips and knees flex when the neck is flexed) support it, but they are insensitive. Their absence does not exclude meningitis, so a suggestive history alone is enough to treat. Jamie's headache built up over 4 hours, which points away from subarachnoid haemorrhage. She has never had any vaccines, so she has no protection against pneumococcus, meningococcus or Haemophilus influenzae type b. A petechial or purpuric rash suggests meningococcal disease. Jamie has none, but a rash can appear later, so the skin needs checking again.

Structuring the headache history

Characterise the headache (onset, site, character, radiation, severity, timing, relieving and aggravating factors), then ask cluster questions that rule each cause in or out:

  • Infection: fever, rigors, neck stiffness, photophobia, rash, vomiting, and risk factors (vaccination, splenectomy, immunosuppression, travel, sick contacts).
  • Haemorrhage: thunderclap onset, a sentinel headache, head trauma (extradural, subdural).
  • Encephalitis: confusion, behaviour change, seizures, memory disturbance.
  • Raised intracranial pressure (tumour, IIH): worse lying down, on waking or with coughing; visual obscurations; vomiting.
  • Posterior circulation stroke: vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, limb weakness.
  • Primary headaches: migraine (aura, previous episodes), cluster (unilateral orbital pain with tearing), tension-type (band-like).
  • Others: GCA and angle-closure glaucoma (unlikely at 18), TMJ dysfunction, dehydration and hypoglycaemia.

Antibiotics first; CT only if needed

In a patient who looks unwell with suspected bacterial meningitis, take blood cultures and start dexamethasone and antibiotics at once. Do not wait for imaging or LP. A CT brain is needed before LP only when there is a contraindication: reduced or falling GCS, focal neurological signs, seizures or papilloedema (and immunocompromise in many protocols). Jamie had none, so LP could go ahead without CT once platelets and coagulation were confirmed normal. The CSF Gram stain and PCR are still useful in the hours after antibiotics are given.

Interpreting the CSF

CSFBacterialViralTB or fungal
AppearanceTurbidClearClear or slightly cloudy
White cellsHigh, neutrophilsRaised, lymphocytesRaised, lymphocytes
ProteinHighNormal or mildly raisedHigh
Glucose (CSF:plasma ratio)LowNormalLow

Jamie's CSF is turbid, with a raised opening pressure, 2400 white cells (90% neutrophils), protein 2.1 g/L and a glucose ratio of about 0.21. Gram-positive diplococci identify Streptococcus pneumoniae; meningococci are Gram-negative diplococci. Minimal red cells argue against subarachnoid haemorrhage. Her bloods show sepsis with a mild lactic acidosis and dehydration. Her observations show sepsis getting worse (yellow zone RR, BP, HR and temperature), which needs senior and ICU review.

Management (eTG Antibiotic: Meningitis)

  • Resuscitate: DRSABCD, IV access, careful fluid resuscitation with reassessment, analgesia and antiemetics.
  • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, then 6-hourly for 4 days. It is continued when pneumococcus is confirmed or suspected, because it reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis.
  • Empirical antibiotic: ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly. Benzylpenicillin for Listeria is added only for patients who are older, immunocompromised, pregnant or alcohol-dependent, which does not apply to Jamie.
  • Pneumococcus suspected (Gram-positive diplococci): eTG adds vancomycin to ceftriaxone until susceptibilities are known, because of cephalosporin-resistant strains. Then change to directed therapy with infectious diseases advice.
  • Monitoring and disposition: hourly neurological observations, fluid balance and sodium; admit under medicine or ID, with ICU if she keeps deteriorating.
  • Public health: invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable. Close contacts do not need prophylaxis, unlike meningococcal and Hib disease.

Safety netting and follow-up

Nurses escalate a falling GCS, confusion, seizures, new focal signs, unequal pupils, a new rash, worsening haemodynamics, and worsening headache or vomiting. Hearing loss is a common complication of pneumococcal meningitis, so a hearing test is arranged before or soon after discharge. Catch-up vaccination follows the Australian Immunisation Handbook, through her GP. Her GP also reviews her after discharge, and she may need help with her VCE, such as special consideration.
points: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Always ask about and look for a non-blanching rash, which suggests meningococcal disease.
In an unwell patient, take blood cultures and give dexamethasone and IV ceftriaxone straight away. Never delay them for CT or LP.
CT before LP is needed only for reduced GCS, focal signs, seizures or papilloedema. Without these, go straight to LP once platelets and coagulation are known to be normal.
A bacterial CSF is turbid, with a neutrophil pleocytosis, high protein and a low glucose ratio. Gram-positive diplococci mean pneumococcus; Gram-negative diplococci mean meningococcus.

eTG: dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or before the first dose, then 6-hourly for 4 days, plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly; add vancomycin when pneumococcus is suspected, until susceptibilities are known.
Invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable, but contacts need no prophylaxis. Arrange a hearing test and catch-up vaccination.
